definition: A change in cellular membrane potential associated with electrical activation.
The electrical recovery process following depolarisation.
The specialised conduction network that normally activates the ventricles rapidly.
A physical skin contact used to acquire an electrical potential.
A defined electrical viewpoint formed from a potential difference.
For simultaneous bipolar limb-lead signals, lead II = lead I + lead III.
The plane describing right–left and superior–inferior directions.
The six standard frontal-plane limb-lead axes arranged around the heart.
The component of an electrical vector along a chosen lead axis.
The six chest leads V1–V6, which view electrical activity in the horizontal plane.
The reference potential derived from the three active limb electrodes for the chest leads.
An anatomical space between adjacent ribs.
A QRS complex that is entirely negative.
The junction between the end of QRS and the ST segment.
A measured period defined by specified waveform boundaries.
The horizontal recording scale, usually expressed in mm/s.
The vertical calibration, usually expressed in mm/mV.
A known signal displayed to indicate the recording scale.
The time between corresponding points on successive ventricular complexes.
The number of ventricular activations per minute.
A rhythm with approximately consistent successive cycle lengths.
Time from P-wave onset to QRS onset.
Time from the beginning to the end of ventricular depolarisation.
A descriptive term for prolonged ventricular activation, interpreted using the relevant task-specific threshold.
Time from QRS onset to the end of the T wave.
A heart-rate-corrected estimate of QT using a named correction formula.
QTc = QT divided by the square root of RR, with RR in seconds.
A rhythm originating from the sinus node, recognised using appropriate atrial activation and timing.
Activation spreading through the atria in a direction opposite to the usual sinus sequence.
A relationship in which each relevant atrial activation is associated with one ventricular activation.
The changing relative R and S amplitudes across the chest leads.
An ECG pattern that may occur without disease in an appropriate context, but still requires careful assessment.
A relationship in which compared waveform directions are similar; its significance depends on the feature and leads being assessed.
The overall frontal-plane direction of ventricular depolarisation.
An axis more leftward than the usual adult −30° boundary.
An axis more rightward than the usual adult +90° boundary.
A complex whose positive contribution exceeds its negative contribution overall.
A regional axis estimate based on the signs of selected perpendicular limb leads.
A lead whose polarity helps determine which side of a category boundary the axis lies on.
A QRS complex with approximately balanced positive and negative components.
An axis estimate using a balanced lead and the polarity of a lead at 90° to it.
An axis that cannot be meaningfully assigned from the available frontal-plane QRS balance.
A 180° region of possible vector directions constrained by one lead’s polarity.
Incorrect connection of labelled electrodes, potentially altering ECG appearances.
Considering several possible explanations for a described ECG finding.
A sinus-origin rhythm with a rate above the usual adult resting range.
Variation in timing between sinus-origin activations.
An atrial rhythm pattern with changing P-wave morphology and irregular atrial timing.
An atrial depolarisation arising earlier than expected outside the sinus node.
A P wave partly or wholly obscured by another waveform.
Altered ventricular activation of a supraventricular impulse through an abnormal conduction pattern.
An organised atrial tachycardia arising from a localised non-sinus origin.
Gradual acceleration that can occur with an automatic tachycardia mechanism.
The relation between the number of atrial activations and conducted ventricular activations.
Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia, involving re-entry through AV nodal pathways.
Atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia using an accessory pathway as part of its circuit.
An accessory pathway without manifest antegrade pre-excitation on the sinus ECG, often conducting retrogradely.
A subsidiary junctional rhythm that activates the heart when higher pacemaker activity is too slow or fails to arrive in time.
A junctional rhythm with increased automaticity relative to the competing sinus pacemaker.
Independent activation of atria and ventricles.
Disorganised atrial electrical activation without a consistent repeating discrete P-wave pattern.
The irregular atrial electrical activity associated with AF.
A rhythm description in which successive cycle lengths vary without a repeating pattern.
An organised rapid atrial tachyarrhythmia, commonly sustained by macro-re-entry.
A repetitive atrial deflection generated during atrial flutter.
Two atrial activations for each conducted ventricular activation.
A later impulse from a subsidiary pacemaker when the expected dominant impulse is absent or delayed.
Failure of a sinus impulse to reach and activate the atria; the sinus discharge is not directly visible on a surface ECG.
Delayed conduction within a subdivision of the left bundle system, inferred from a characteristic activation pattern.
An ST–T alteration resulting from an abnormal ventricular depolarisation sequence.
A typical Mobitz I sequence of progressive AV conduction delay before a non-conducted atrial impulse.
An AV conduction pattern with two atrial depolarisations for every ventricular response.
Advanced AV block with multiple consecutive non-conducted atrial impulses; state the actual observed pattern.
A conduction disturbance in which atrial impulses fail to reach the ventricles during the observed interval.
The counted relation of atrial depolarisations to ventricular responses in a defined ECG segment.
An interval without ventricular depolarisation; distinguish it from absent atrial activity and artefact.
A premature beat inserted between baseline beats without the usual ensuing compensatory pause.
Two consecutive ventricular premature beats.
A supraventricular impulse that successfully activates the ventricles during an otherwise ventricular rhythm.
A QRS produced by combined ventricular activation from competing wavefronts.
QRS complexes with the same dominant polarity across the chest leads.
Ventricular tachycardia with a broadly uniform QRS appearance from beat to beat in a given lead.
Ventricular tachycardia with varying QRS morphology from beat to beat.
A polymorphic VT associated with a long-QT repolarisation context and characteristic changing QRS axis/amplitude.
A rhythm maintained by a subsidiary pacemaker when dominant impulses are too slow or fail to arrive.
A ventricular response in AF that becomes unusually regular, requiring assessment for pacing, block or another pacemaker.
Cycle-length-dependent aberrant conduction classically associated with a long–short RR sequence in AF.
An early atrial depolarisation that is not followed by a ventricular QRS response.
A repeating atrial pattern in which baseline atrial beats alternate with premature atrial beats.
A changing proportion of atrial impulses producing ventricular responses.
A tachycardia originating in atrial tissue, often with organised atrial activity distinct from ordinary sinus rhythm.
A tachycardia with widened ventricular complexes; it describes activation without alone specifying origin.
A conduction change that emerges at particular cycle lengths or rates.
Successful supraventricular activation of the ventricles during an otherwise ventricular rhythm.
A QRS appearance created by simultaneous contributions from different ventricular activation wavefronts.
The earliest phase of ventricular depolarisation represented at QRS onset.
A markedly abnormal frontal QRS direction; interpret it together with morphology and lead validity.
A set of plausible mechanisms considered against the available evidence.
The degree of support for an interpretation, distinct from whether a label is technically possible.
A recorded electrical stimulus from a pacemaker, often called a pacing spike.
Pacing between two nearby electrodes on a lead, often producing a smaller surface artefact than unipolar pacing.
Pacing behaviour in which appropriately sensed intrinsic activity can inhibit an otherwise due stimulus.
A device timing response in which sensed atrial events can be followed by ventricular pacing within programmed rules.
Successful depolarisation of the intended cardiac chamber by a pacing stimulus.
The minimum stimulus output needed to produce reliable depolarisation under specified conditions.
Failure of a device to detect intrinsic activity that should influence its operation.
Detection of signals that should not be treated as the intended intrinsic cardiac event, potentially altering pacing behaviour.
Slurred initial QRS deflection caused by early ventricular myocardial activation during pre-excitation.
An additional electrical connection that can bypass part of the normal atrioventricular conduction route.
AV re-entry with antegrade conduction through the usual AV system and retrograde return through an accessory pathway.
Atrial fibrillation with antegrade ventricular activation through an accessory pathway.
Electrical conduction from atria towards ventricles.
An ECG appearance resembling infarction that can arise from another activation or structural mechanism.
A downward slurred initial QRS deflection caused by the direction of pre-excited ventricular activation.
Insufficient myocardial oxygen supply relative to demand.
Myocardial damage evidenced clinically by troponin above its reference limit; acute injury shows a rise or fall.
Leads viewing neighbouring anatomical regions.
An opposite-direction ST change in leads viewing a region opposite the principal pattern.
Additional leads V7–V9 placed to view the posterior left ventricular region.
A disproportionately broad, prominent T wave that may accompany early regional ischaemia.
A characteristic anterior T-wave warning pattern requiring clinical interpretation.
The first negative QRS deflection before any positive R wave.
ST–T direction opposite the main QRS direction.
An ECG pattern that can reflect right ventricular pressure or load, with characteristic repolarisation and sometimes conduction changes.
S wave in I, Q wave in III and inverted T wave in III.
PR-segment displacement below the chosen baseline, which can support pericardial inflammation in context.
A J-point/repolarisation pattern that is often a normal variant but requires contextual interpretation.
Beat-to-beat alternation in the amplitude or axis of ECG complexes.
Fluid accumulation within the pericardial space.
Inflammation involving the myocardium.
The underlying cause of a clinical finding or disease.
SV1 plus the larger RV5 or RV6 amplitude; one ECG voltage criterion used for LVH assessment.
Left ventricular hypertrophy; anatomical enlargement of myocardial mass, imperfectly predicted by ECG criteria.
The relative contribution of ventricular electrical forces to the surface QRS.
Right ventricular hypertrophy, which cannot be measured directly from an ECG.
The final portion of the P wave, particularly assessed in V1.
A P wave with two distinct peaks.
Deposition or accumulation of material within myocardial tissue.
A small initial R, intervening S and terminal positive deflection in a right precordial lead.
A relationship between ECG changes and a disease outside the primary electrical system.
Right-sided cardiac orientation, assessed using anatomical and clinical evidence as well as ECG clues.
Electrode interchange that changes recorded lead relationships.
A physiological or electrical change associated with medication exposure.
Ventricular tachycardia with alternating QRS axis/morphology, associated with several causes.
An increased extracellular potassium concentration, established biochemically.
A severe broad merging QRS–T morphology that is not a numerical potassium measurement.
A deflection after the T wave; prominence has several possible associations.
An interval extending to the end of a U wave rather than the T wave.
A J-wave deflection near the QRS–ST junction, classically associated with hypothermia but not specific.
Hormonal conditions that can modify rate, conduction or repolarisation.
A pattern that can occur without disease in a defined clinical context.
A physiological electrical or structural change associated with athletic conditioning.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a myocardial disease established using clinical and structural criteria.
The observable expression of a condition, such as an ECG or imaging pattern.
Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, potentially involving the right, left or both ventricles.
A small terminal depolarisation signal after the principal QRS, whose identification requires care.
A characteristic right-precordial ST morphology requiring clinical interpretation.
A similar-appearing pattern produced by an alternative cause rather than the presumed inherited syndrome.
A method for estimating T-wave end using a tangent to its terminal downslope.
An inherited repolarisation disorder assessed using clinical, ECG and sometimes genetic evidence.
QT lengthening associated with non-inherited contributors such as drugs or electrolyte disturbance.
A shortened QT/QTc observation requiring measurement and clinical assessment.
Electrocardiogram: a recording of cardiac electrical potential differences measured at the body surface.
The waveform representing ventricular depolarisation; its onset and end define QRS duration.
The ventricular depolarisation complex, comprising any Q, R and S deflections that are present.
The surface ECG waveform representing atrial depolarisation.
The surface ECG waveform representing ventricular repolarisation.
The portion from the end of QRS, at the J point, to the beginning of the T wave.
The portion from the end of the P wave to the beginning of QRS; distinct from the entire PR interval.
Atrioventricular node: part of the conduction system that normally delays activation between atria and ventricles.
The sinoatrial pacemaker region that normally initiates atrial electrical activation.
The two upper cardiac chambers; atrial electrical activation normally precedes ventricular activation.
The two lower cardiac chambers; their depolarisation produces the QRS complex.
The muscular tissue of the heart.
Atrial fibrillation: disorganised atrial electrical activity without consistent discrete P waves; the ventricular response is often irregular.
Supraventricular tachycardia: a tachycardia arising from or involving structures above the ventricular myocardium; mechanisms differ.
Ventricular tachycardia: a rapid rhythm originating in the ventricles; surface ECG clues support interpretation but must be contextualised.
Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic ventricular electrical activity without organised QRS complexes.
Right bundle branch block: delayed right ventricular activation producing a characteristic QRS pattern.
Left bundle branch block: delayed left ventricular activation producing a characteristic QRS pattern.
Bundle branch block: impaired conduction through a major branch of the His–Purkinje system.
Wolff–Parkinson–White: a ventricular pre-excitation pattern involving an accessory pathway; the ECG pattern alone is distinct from symptomatic WPW syndrome.
Atrioventricular block: delayed or interrupted conduction of atrial impulses towards the ventricles.
The interval from the onset of QRS to the end of the T wave, encompassing ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation.
The time between consecutive R waves; in a regular rhythm, rate in beats/min equals 60 divided by RR in seconds.
A heart-rate correction estimate: QTc = QT divided by the cube root of RR, with QT and RR in seconds.
Beats per minute, a unit of heart rate.
Millivolt: one thousandth of a volt, used to express ECG signal amplitude.
Millisecond: one thousandth of a second, used to express ECG timing.
Relating to insufficient blood supply for tissue metabolic needs; an ECG pattern alone does not establish its cause.
Acute myocardial injury accompanied by evidence of acute myocardial ischaemia; ECG, biomarkers and clinical findings are interpreted together.
A cardiac injury biomarker; an elevated result alone does not establish coronary infarction.
Inflammation of the pericardium; ECG changes can support assessment but are not sufficient alone.
Obstruction of the pulmonary arterial circulation, commonly by thrombus; ECG findings are often nonspecific.
A low blood potassium concentration, which may alter repolarisation and promote arrhythmias.
A slow heart rate; its significance depends on rhythm mechanism and clinical context.
A fast heart rate; rate alone does not establish the rhythm mechanism.
A recorded signal distortion that does not represent the cardiac electrical event being interpreted.
Ventricular activation occurring early through a pathway that bypasses the usual AV nodal delay.
An abnormality of cardiac rhythm, rate, impulse formation or conduction.
Propagation of an electrical impulse through cardiac tissue.
Altered ventricular activation of a supraventricular impulse, often through functional or fixed bundle branch conduction delay.
An upward displacement of the ST segment relative to the chosen baseline; interpretation depends on leads, magnitude, morphology and clinical context.
A downward displacement of the ST segment relative to baseline; it has several possible causes.
The interval from the start of P to the start of QRS when used as PR interval; PR segment refers only to the portion after P.

The mean direction of an electrical vector; the frontal QRS axis describes the net direction of ventricular depolarisation in the frontal plane. In a plotted strip, the time axis instead shows elapsed time; this is distinct from the electrical QRS axis.
Recording and interpreting cardiac electrical potential differences at the body surface; ECG is the resulting electrocardiogram.
The usual cardiac pacemaker region in the right atrium; its impulses normally initiate atrial depolarisation.
The AV node, which normally delays conduction between atrial activation and the ventricular conduction system.
The conducting connection from the AV nodal region to the right and left bundle branches.
Specialised conducting tissue that distributes activation rapidly through ventricular myocardium.
A time-dependent change in a cell’s membrane voltage produced by coordinated ion movement through membrane channels.
The voltage difference across a cell membrane between activation events; altered electrolyte gradients can affect excitability.
A period following activation during which tissue cannot be re-excited normally or responds differently to another impulse.
The ability of specialised cardiac cells to initiate electrical impulses spontaneously.
A rhythm mechanism in which activation repeatedly circulates through a pathway that can re-excite recovered tissue.
Electrical activity arising from afterdepolarisations associated with a preceding action potential.
An additional membrane-voltage oscillation during or after repolarisation that can, in some circumstances, initiate another impulse.
The speed at which an activation wave propagates through tissue; different cardiac tissues conduct at different speeds.
Electrical activation of atrial myocardium, normally represented by the P wave.
Electrical activation of ventricular myocardium, represented by the QRS complex.
Recovery of ventricular electrical state after depolarisation; the T wave is its principal surface ECG representation.
Electrical recovery of the atria, usually obscured by ventricular electrical activity in the surface ECG.
The reference level used to describe positive and negative ECG deflections; baseline choice matters when measuring segment displacement.
A portion of the ECG waveform that moves above or below the selected baseline.
The vertical size of a waveform, expressed as voltage or grid height at a stated gain.
The shape and configuration of a waveform; distinct from its duration, timing or rate.
Whether a waveform is predominantly positive, negative or biphasic in a particular lead.
A waveform with both positive and negative components.
A lead that records the potential difference between two electrode locations.
A lead that compares an exploring electrode with a constructed reference rather than a single opposite electrode.
The aVR, aVL and aVF limb leads, whose reference construction augments the recorded signal.
Augmented right-arm limb lead, oriented approximately −150 degrees in the frontal hexaxial reference system.
Augmented left-arm limb lead, oriented approximately −30 degrees in the frontal hexaxial reference system.
Augmented foot limb lead, oriented approximately +90 degrees in the frontal hexaxial reference system.
The transverse electrical view principally represented by the precordial chest leads.
The first precordial lead; its electrode is normally placed in the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border.
The second precordial lead; its electrode is normally placed in the fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border.
The third precordial lead; its electrode is placed midway between correctly located V2 and V4 electrodes.
The fourth precordial lead; its electrode is normally placed in the fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line.
The fifth precordial lead; its electrode is placed at the anterior axillary line, horizontally level with V4.
The sixth precordial lead; its electrode is placed at the midaxillary line, horizontally level with V4 and V5.
The anatomical edge of the sternum, used as a reference when positioning chest electrodes.
A vertical anatomical line through the midpoint of the clavicle, used when locating the V4 electrode.
A vertical anatomical line at the anterior axillary fold, used for V5 placement.
A vertical line through the middle of the axilla, used for V6 placement.
Slow movement of the ECG baseline, often from respiration, movement or electrode contact changes.
Electrical interference from skeletal muscle activity that can obscure cardiac waveforms.
Electrical noise related to the alternating-current power supply; it can resemble rapid repetitive activity.
The time between successive P waves, used to assess atrial rate and timing.
The first positive deflection in a QRS complex.
A negative deflection following an R wave in the QRS complex.
A second positive QRS deflection after an intervening negative deflection, often written R′.
The precordial region where the R and S amplitudes are approximately equal; position varies with anatomy, activation and electrode placement.
An estimate of the algebraic balance of positive and negative QRS deflections in a lead, useful for axis reasoning.
Delayed conduction through the left anterior fascicle, associated with a characteristic frontal-plane activation pattern.
Delayed conduction through the left posterior fascicle; rightward axis alone is insufficient to establish it.
Conduction impairment involving two major fascicular pathways; interpretation requires the full ECG pattern.
Second-degree AV block with a Wenckebach conduction pattern, classically progressive PR prolongation before a non-conducted P wave.
Second-degree AV block with intermittent failed conduction without the classic Wenckebach PR sequence; a fixed 2:1 ratio alone does not establish this type.
A visible atrial depolarisation without a corresponding conducted ventricular complex; its cause requires timing and rhythm analysis.
A rhythm arising from the AV junctional region; P waves may be absent, hidden or retrograde.
An early ventricular-origin beat, often with a broad abnormal QRS and altered repolarisation; timing and full morphology matter.
A longer interval after a premature beat; a full compensatory pause spans approximately two baseline cycles, but not all premature beats produce one.
A repeating pattern in which one type of beat alternates with another, such as a sinus beat followed by a premature beat.
A repeating pattern in which a particular premature event occurs every third beat.
A ventricular premature event occurring during the preceding T wave; the significance depends on the substrate and context.
A late protective ventricular impulse when higher pacemakers or conduction do not provide the expected activation.
A ventricular-origin rhythm, commonly slower than ventricular tachycardia; rate labels alone do not establish mechanism.
A ventricular-origin rhythm faster than a typical slow ventricular escape, with rate and mechanism assessed in context.
Propagation of atrial activation towards the ventricles through the atrioventricular conduction system.
Atrioventricular: relating to the atria, ventricles or their electrical connection.
Premature ventricular complex, an early ventricular-origin beat.
Premature atrial complex, an early atrial-origin depolarisation that may conduct normally, aberrantly or not at all.
Pulmonary embolism; its ECG findings are often nonspecific and cannot confirm or exclude it alone.
Coronary artery disease; ECG abnormalities may support assessment but do not directly measure coronary anatomy.
Acute coronary syndrome, a clinical framework requiring symptoms, ECG and other relevant evidence.
ST-elevation myocardial infarction, a clinical classification involving qualifying ECG findings in the appropriate setting; ST elevation alone has other causes.
Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, requiring evidence of acute injury and ischaemia without the STEMI ECG classification.
Sudden cardiac death; an outcome with several possible underlying mechanisms and substrates.
Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, an inherited arrhythmia disorder whose resting ECG may be unremarkable.
Long-QT syndrome, an inherited or acquired context of abnormal repolarisation; QT measurement and clinical assessment are needed.
A deflection or notch near the junction between QRS and ST; appearance and clinical significance depend on context.
A traditional description of tall peaked P-wave morphology associated with right atrial abnormality; it does not independently prove chamber enlargement.
A traditional description of a broad or notched P wave associated with left atrial abnormality; morphology is not a direct chamber-size measurement.
Anatomical enlargement of an atrial chamber; ECG criteria suggest atrial abnormality but do not directly measure its size.
Increased ventricular muscle mass; voltage and repolarisation patterns can support assessment but have imperfect sensitivity and specificity.
The sac surrounding the heart; its inflammation or fluid accumulation can influence the ECG in different ways.
Disease involving ion-channel function, potentially altering cardiac electrical behaviour without an obvious structural abnormality.
A disorder of heart muscle structure or function; ECG patterns may prompt further investigation but do not define all features alone.
The proportion of people with a genetic variant who show a related observable phenotype; age and other factors can influence it.
The extent or form of an observable phenotype among people with the same underlying genetic association.
The proportion of people with a target condition who have a positive test result; a low sensitivity limits exclusion by a negative result.
The proportion without a target condition who have a negative test result; imperfect specificity permits false-positive results.
The estimated likelihood of a condition before considering the test result; it changes how a finding is interpreted.
The proportion of positive test results that correspond to the target condition in the population being assessed.
Distortion of an apparent relationship by another factor associated with the variables being studied.
Differences in measurements or interpretations between observers or repeated assessments.
A statistical interval indicating uncertainty around an estimate under a specified method; it is not a range containing a fixed proportion of individual values.
A sample selected because participants are readily available, which can limit representativeness.
A study that observes exposures or outcomes without assigning the exposure experimentally; causal interpretation requires care.
Electrical activity arising in the atria, represented by P waves, flutter waves or other atrial signals depending on the rhythm.
The sequence of electrical depolarisation through ventricular tissue; it generates the QRS complex.
The timing and rate of ventricular activation in relation to the atrial rhythm and AV conduction.
The sequence of ventricular events; the phrase can describe their timing without necessarily proving a ventricular pacemaker origin.
A rapid rhythm originating in ventricular tissue; distinguishing it from supraventricular tachycardia with broad complexes requires systematic assessment.
An electrical activation originating in or spreading through the atria.
The rate, regularity and activation pattern of the atria, assessed separately from the ventricular sequence when possible.
A major conducting pathway carrying activation from the His bundle towards a ventricle.
Depolarisation spreading through atrial myocardium, normally producing the P wave.
The six frontal-plane ECG views I, II, III, aVR, aVL and aVF, derived from limb electrode potentials.
Electrical stimulation intended to activate a ventricle; a visible marker may precede a paced QRS, but actual pacing artefacts can be very small.
An identifiable atrial depolarisation or atrial waveform considered when comparing atrial and ventricular timing.
The duration from the earliest QRS onset to the latest QRS end; width should be assessed with appropriate calibration and across relevant leads.
Specialised cardiac tissue that initiates and distributes electrical activation through the sinus node, AV junction, His bundle, branches and Purkinje network.
How reliably a tracing represents the intended cardiac signal, considering electrode placement, contact, calibration and interference.
The beginning of ventricular depolarisation as identified on the ECG; it is the starting boundary for QRS and QT measurements.
The number of atrial activation events per minute, estimated from atrial cycle length or a timed atrial count.
A slow sinus-origin rhythm; its clinical significance depends on symptoms, medicines, physiological setting and other findings.
The symptoms, history, examination, medicines, timing and additional tests needed to interpret an ECG finding appropriately.
Relevant health findings in relatives, including inherited disease or unexplained early death, which may affect interpretation and investigation.
The shape and configuration of ventricular depolarisation in particular leads, distinct from QRS duration alone.
A T wave directed below the baseline in a lead; its significance depends on the lead, age, activation pattern, serial findings and clinical context.
A description of observed electrical features; a pattern is not automatically a complete clinical diagnosis.
Small QRS amplitudes under a specified lead-based criterion; correct gain, recording quality and clinical context must be checked.
The order and timing in which cardiac regions depolarise, affecting the direction and shape of recorded waveforms.
Changes in tissue electrical state associated with impulse formation, propagation and recovery; electrical organisation does not itself prove effective circulation.
A mean electrical axis outside a stated reference range; lead polarity, boundary leads and recording quality should be checked before labelling it.
A continuous recording of one or more leads used to examine timing and rhythm; it does not replace all the information in a 12-lead ECG.
A clinical description of impaired electrical propagation; the ECG pattern, level, persistence and clinical significance require assessment.
Leads II, III and aVF, which view the heart from inferior frontal-plane orientations.
Leads viewing lateral electrical forces, commonly I, aVL, V5 and V6; interpretations depend on the complete ECG.
A conventional regional label often applied to V1–V2; surface lead groupings are not exact maps of individual myocardial segments.
A conventional regional description commonly applied to precordial leads over the anterior chest, interpreted with the full lead pattern.
The reference-positive end of a lead vector; a depolarisation vector towards it generally produces a positive deflection.
A waveform movement below the chosen isoelectric baseline in a particular lead.
A waveform movement above the chosen isoelectric baseline in a particular lead.
The mean frontal-plane direction of ventricular depolarisation, estimated using the limb-lead system.
The time from a ventricular R wave to the next related P wave; useful in describing atrial–ventricular timing during some tachycardias.
The signed component of a resultant electrical vector along a lead direction; near-perpendicular vectors can produce a small net deflection.
Independent atrial and ventricular pacemakers operating at similar rates; dissociation alone does not establish complete AV block.
The volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute; the surface ECG does not directly measure it.
The volume of blood ejected by a ventricle with a beat; an electrical tracing does not directly determine that volume.
Blood supply through the coronary circulation to the myocardium; an ECG records electrical effects rather than flow itself.
A heart-muscle cell whose electrical activation and recovery contribute to the recorded cardiac signal.
The voltage difference across a cell membrane, determined by ion distributions and membrane permeability.
A membrane protein permitting sodium-ion movement; sodium-channel behaviour contributes to cardiac excitability and conduction.
A membrane protein permitting potassium-ion movement; several potassium currents contribute to repolarisation.
A membrane protein permitting calcium-ion movement, contributing to electrical activation and excitation–contraction coupling in cardiac tissues.
An electrically charged substance in solution; changes in blood electrolyte concentrations can influence cardiac electrical behaviour.
A low blood calcium concentration; it may affect repolarisation, but the ECG cannot determine the calcium level by itself.
An elevated blood calcium concentration; ECG effects require clinical and laboratory interpretation.
A low core body temperature that can alter rate, conduction and repolarisation; an ECG pattern alone does not establish the temperature.
Regulation of cardiac activity by autonomic nervous-system influences, assessed with appropriate physiological methods rather than a single ECG label.
Autonomic activity that commonly slows sinus rate and influences AV conduction; its net effect depends on the physiological setting.
Autonomic activity that can increase pacemaker rate and influence conduction, excitability and contractility.
Parasympathetic influence mediated through vagal pathways; it can affect sinus and AV nodal behaviour.
The physiological processes linking electrical activation to mechanical contraction; the two events are related but not identical.
An alteration in the recovery-related portion of the ECG, including ST–T changes; multiple physiological and pathological causes are possible.
Changes involving the ST segment and/or T wave; describe distribution, magnitude, shape and context before attributing a cause.
A repolarisation alteration not simply explained as a consequence of a changed ventricular depolarisation sequence.
A conduction pattern that changes with cycle length or rate; timing and refractory behaviour can affect ventricular morphology.
Relating to the right ventricle; a regional description does not by itself imply enlargement, strain or disease.
Relating to the left ventricle; ECG voltage and morphology are indirect evidence rather than direct anatomical measurements.
Premature atrial activity that may conduct normally, conduct aberrantly or fail to conduct to the ventricles.
Premature ventricular-origin electrical activity, assessed by timing, morphology and relationship to other events.
Occurrence of an event earlier than expected from the preceding rhythm; distinguish it from a late escape event.
The interval between a preceding reference beat and a premature beat, used when analysing ectopic timing.
A temporary absence of expected sinus atrial activity; determine whether a hidden premature P wave or another mechanism explains the apparent gap.
Failure of a generated impulse to propagate out of its site of formation; surface ECG evidence may support but not directly record the pacemaker discharge.
An impulse influencing tissue refractoriness or subsequent conduction without producing a fully visible conducted response.
The atrioventricular nodal and neighbouring conducting region; junctional rhythms can activate atria retrogradely and ventricles antegradely.
Propagating in the usual forward direction through the pathway being described.
Propagating in the reverse direction relative to the usual activation sequence.
A circuit description in which activation travels forward through the usual AV conduction system and returns by an accessory route in a typical orthodromic AVRT mechanism.
A circuit description in which ventricular activation travels forward through an accessory pathway in an antidromic AVRT mechanism, usually producing broad complexes.
The combined ability of repolarising currents to maintain recovery; medicines, electrolytes and inherited factors may reduce this capacity.
Present from birth or arising during development; congenital does not always mean inherited.
Developing because of factors arising during life, such as medicines or electrolyte disturbances, rather than being solely congenital.
A finding associated with an outcome in an appropriate evidence context; it is not automatically a prediction for an individual.
A defined finding or combination used within a diagnostic framework; population, measurement and clinical context affect its application.
The set of plausible explanations for an observed finding that must be compared using further evidence.
A measurable biological indicator used as evidence about a process or condition; a single result must be interpreted in context.
An ECG assessed alongside recordings obtained at other times to identify evolving, resolving or stable changes.
The set of leads in which a finding appears, considered with anatomical orientation, reciprocal findings and technical factors.
The anatomical positioning of recording electrodes; incorrect positioning can change apparent morphology and interpretation.
An ECG recorded from body-surface electrodes, reflecting the combined effects of cardiac activity and the recording geometry.
The bipolar limb lead defined by left-arm potential minus right-arm potential, oriented at 0 degrees in the usual frontal reference system.
The bipolar limb lead defined by left-leg potential minus right-arm potential, oriented approximately +60 degrees.
The bipolar limb lead defined by left-leg potential minus left-arm potential, oriented approximately +120 degrees.
A conceptual model linking the three bipolar limb-lead views; it is a geometrical teaching model rather than the literal shape of the heart.
Computational methods for organising and analysing biological data, including genomic and transcriptomic information.
The study of RNA transcripts expressed in biological samples, with careful attention to experimental design and analysis.
